worst_places.quote: "The If-Match ETag does not match the current resource ETag, indicating the resource was modified by another client since the request was prepared"
worst_places.problem: http-rest-quiz-5 keys 409 Conflict as the correct status for a failed If-Match precondition. Both articles in this same zone teach 412: 03-caching-and-headers.md shows `# Если кто-то уже изменил документ:` / `HTTP/1.1 412 Precondition Failed`, and 09-http-rest-interview-questions.md Q10 says `При несовпадении → 412 Precondition Failed`. RFC 9110 §13.1.1 agrees with the articles, not the quiz. A reader who studies article 03, then answers this quiz item correctly, has been taught two contradictory rules and the wrong one is the one that scores a point. The explanation doubles down: `409 Conflict ... commonly caused by ETag mismatch in optimistic locking`.
worst_places.before:
Q: A REST API returns HTTP 409 Conflict for a PUT request to update a resource. Which scenario best explains why this status code was chosen?
[correct] The If-Match ETag does not match the current resource ETag, indicating the resource was modified by another client since the request was prepared
Explanation: 409 Conflict indicates a request conflict with the current state, commonly caused by ETag mismatch in optimistic locking—the resource was modified elsewhere since the client's last read.
worst_places.after:
Q: A REST API returns HTTP 412 Precondition Failed for a PUT request that carried `If-Match: "abc123"`. Why this status code?
[correct] The If-Match ETag does not match the current resource ETag. Someone else changed the resource after this client read it, so the precondition failed.
Explanation: `If-Match` is a precondition. When it does not match, the correct code is 412 Precondition Failed — this is optimistic locking. 409 Conflict is for a conflict with the resource state that has no precondition header behind it, such as a duplicate email on registration. 404 means the resource does not exist, 503 means the server is overloaded, 403 means no permission.

Q: HTTP/2 introduces server push, allowing the server to send resources to the client without waiting for explicit requests. Which of the following is a primary advantage of server push over HTTP/1.1's approach?
[correct] Reduces round-trip time by eliminating the request-response cycle for predictable dependencies
worst_places.after:
Q: HTTP/2 server push let the server send style.css before the client asked for it. It saved a round trip — yet Chrome removed it in 2022 and HTTP/3 dropped it from the spec. What replaced it?
[correct] 103 Early Hints: the server sends `Link: </style.css>; rel=preload` early, and the browser decides whether it already has the file cached
(Distractors: HPACK header compression / stream prioritization / domain sharding.)
Explanation: Server push saved one round trip for predictable dependencies, but the server could not know what was already in the client's cache, so it wasted bandwidth on files the browser already had. 103 Early Hints gives the same head start and lets the browser make the caching decision.

[correct] JWT (JSON Web Tokens) with client-side validation
Explanation: ... Basic auth is stateless but transmits credentials in every request (insecure without HTTPS).
worst_places.after:
Q: You need REST API authentication that is stateless (no session store on the server) AND does not resend the user's password on every request. Which one fits?
[correct] JWT (JSON Web Tokens): the server checks the signature, stores nothing, and the password is sent only once at login
Explanation: JWT is stateless — the server verifies the signature without storing session data. Session cookies need a server-side store, which is stateful. Basic auth is also stateless, but it resends the login and password on every single request, so it fails the second condition. OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow needs server-side state for the authorization code.

worst_places.before: - **"Why is `Vary: Origin` needed?"** — without it, a cache (CDN, proxy) might return a response with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://a.com` to a client with origin `https://b.com`. `Vary: Origin` tells the cache to store separate versions of the response for each origin.
worst_places.after: - **"Why is `Vary: Origin` needed?"** — because the same URL can return a different `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` per caller. Say a cache (a CDN or proxy) stores your response for `https://a.com`. It then hands that same stored copy to a client whose origin is `https://b.com`. The header still says `a.com`, so the browser blocks it. `Vary: Origin` tells the cache to keep one copy per origin instead of one copy total.

patterns: The articles are among the cleanest on the site on sentence length, lead sentences and concept density (B 4.35, C 3.7, D 4.5 — every new idea lands next to a diagram, table or code block), and the single repeating defect is abbreviations. An acronym is expanded in the one article whose title is about it and nowhere else: CORS is spelled out in 04 but bare in 01 and 09; SSE is spelled out by the heading in 08 but used bare four lines earlier in that same file's intro; HoL is expanded in 07 only. Meanwhile the transport-layer set (TCP, TLS, UDP, RTT, QUIC, CDN, DNS) is never expanded anywhere in the zone — RTT is used 11 times in 07 and 9 times in 09 without ever being written as 'round-trip time'. Fixing A is mechanical: one parenthetical at the first use per file, no restructuring.

The quiz layer is built to a different (much lower) standard than everything around it and its defects are structural, not linguistic. Three independent tells let a reader score without knowing HTTP: the key is index 0 in 22/28 items and never 2 or 3; the correct option is the longest option in 14/28; and 10/28 items are near-verbatim repeats of an earlier item. On top of that the bank contradicts the articles it is supposed to test (409 vs 412 for If-Match, Server Push framed as a live advantage the article calls a failed feature) and skips three whole articles (REST principles, pagination, real-time) entirely. Article-level fixes are cosmetic; the quiz needs a rebuild against the article outline.

Both localisations drift from each other in small, load-bearing ways rather than in register. The register is fine — RU is living language, EN is roughly B1-B2 — but each locale carries its own broken code example that the other has correct: RU 03 declares `(_req, res)` then reads `req.headers`, EN 04 has `"PUT", PATCH"` with a missing quote. RU 01 has a garbled phrase (`нафиксировано зачем`) where EN reads fine. In the quiz, the EN explanation for quiz-13 ends with `making option 1 the only correct behavior here` and the RU explanation silently drops that clause. Whatever pass produced these files did not diff the two locales against each other.
